title: Conceptual understanding is a myth
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman challenges one of the central claims used to defend inquiry-based mathematics instruction: that it develops 'conceptual understanding' in a way that explicit teaching cannot. He argues that when researchers attempt to actually measure conceptual understanding, it transforms into 'conceptual knowledge'—which, on close inspection, turns out to be indistinguishable from procedural knowledge. The Crooks and Alibali (2014) review of measurement attempts found the most common 'conceptual' task was reciting a definition of the equals sign, which is ironically a rote recitation task. Ashman further argues that questions designed to test conceptual understanding only work if students haven't been previously taught how to solve them—which means the measure is really about transfer of learning, not some separate cognitive faculty. Since Thorndike established that transfer depends on the degree to which contexts share common elements, the claim that conceptual understanding is a distinct and separately assessable thing dissolves. The piece concludes that rather than arguing about procedures versus concepts, educators should focus on measuring transfer of learning, which is the actual goal.
points: The conceptual/procedural distinction is an empirical myth: when researchers attempt to measure conceptual understanding, it becomes conceptual knowledge, which is functionally indistinguishable from procedural knowledge—suggesting the distinction may be the jangle fallacy (two identical things given different names).

The most common measure of conceptual understanding in mathematics education research is asking students to define what the equals sign means—which is a rote recitation task, undermining the claim that conceptual assessments measure something beyond what explicit teaching provides.

Conceptual questions only work as such if students haven't seen similar question types before; if they have been taught to solve them, the 'conceptual' label is just a different name for a more scaffolded form of procedural practice.

What advocates of conceptual understanding are actually reaching for is transfer of learning—the ability to apply knowledge across contexts with different surface features—and this is the right goal, but it should be named directly rather than dressed up as a distinct cognitive faculty.

Transfer of learning is notoriously difficult to produce, and Thorndike's principle remains: it depends on the degree to which contexts share common elements. We cannot simply learn to think better in the abstract.
quotes: If you begin to participate in the debate about mathematics teaching, two things quickly become apparent. The first is gaslighting. The second feature is a focus on the hocus pocus of conceptual understanding. This is a dodge.

When researchers try to assess conceptual understanding, a strange transformation takes place. Suddenly, it becomes conceptual knowledge. Procedural knowledge and conceptual knowledge are mutually supportive—they would support each other if they were effectively the same thing.

What does 'understanding' look like beyond being able to do and say certain things? Therefore, it is the doing and saying that are measured and these look a lot like knowledge. How, exactly, is this different to procedural knowledge?

Speak to a colleague who has explicitly taught students how to write explanations in examined courses in science, economics or business management and you will realise that this is their daily work. So, is it the explanation that is the critical point that assessing conceptual knowledge? Maybe not.

The procedures these same advocates disparage are far harder to reproduce. At the very least, they involve recalling the procedure and then applying it to a new set of numbers and most of the time, there will be considerably more transfer of learning required than that.

Rather than asking students to recall definitions or fooling ourselves that some kinds of procedural questions really are procedural, whereas others are conceptual, we should focus instead on measuring transfer of learning. Conceptual understanding is a myth.
